FCC 24-112

Released October 18, 2024 
 
In accordance with Section 212 of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 
1996, this Small Entity Compliance Guide (Guide) is intended to help small entities—small businesses, 
small organizations (non-profits), and small governmental jurisdictions—comply with the rules adopted 
in the above-referenced Federal Communications Commission (FCC or Commission) rulemaking 
dockets.  This Guide is not intended to replace or supersede these rules, but to facilitate compliance with 
the rules.  Although we have attempted to cover all parts of the rules that might be especially important 
to small entities, the coverage may not be exhaustive.  This Guide cannot anticipate all situations in 
which the rules apply.  Furthermore, the Commission retains the discretion to adopt case-by-case 
approaches, where appropriate, that may differ from this Guide.  Any decision regarding a particular 
small entity will be based on the statute and any relevant rules. 
In any civil or administrative action against a small entity for a violation of rules, the content of 
the Guide may be considered as evidence of the reasonableness or appropriateness of proposed fines, 
penalties or damages.  Interested parties are free to file comments regarding this Guide in the above 
referenced docket and the appropriateness of its application to a particular situation.  The Commission 
will then consider whether the recommendations or interpretations in the Guide are appropriate in that 
situation.  The Commission may decide to revise this Guide without public notice to reflect changes in 
its approach to implementing a rule, or it may clarify or update the text of the Guide.  Please direct

Synopsis: 
I. Introduction 
In this final rule, we advance our goal 
of ensuring that all Americans can 
access communications services on an 
equal basis by fulfilling the 
Commission’s longstanding 
commitment to establish a 100% 
hearing aid compatibility requirement 
that applies to all future wireless 
handset models offered for sale or use 
in the United States. By our actions in 
this final rule, 48 million Americans 
with hearing loss will be able to choose 
among the same handset models that are 
available to consumers without hearing 
loss. No longer will they be limited in 
their choice of technologies, features, 
and prices available in the handset 
model marketplace. Further, our rules 
will encourage handset manufacturers 
to move away from proprietary

ensure more universal connectivity 
between handset models and hearing 
aids, including over-the-counter hearing 
aids. In order to ensure that older

purchase, we provide for a phase-out

standards. In addition, we strengthen 
wireless handset accessibility to 
encompass not only compatibility that 
benefits consumers who use hearing 
aids, but also a 100% volume control 
requirement for new handsets that 
benefits all consumers with hearing 
loss. Finally, we adopt revised labeling 
and website posting requirements that 
allow consumers to have access to the 
information that they need to make 
informed handset model purchasing 
decisions. 
The revisions that we adopt to our 
hearing aid compatibility rules are 
based in part on the collaborative efforts 
of members of the Hearing Aid 
Compatibility Task Force (HAC Task 
Force), who worked together over a 
period of years to reach a consensus on 
how the Commission could achieve its 
long held goal of a 100% hearing aid 
compatibility benchmark for all handset 
models offered for sale or use in the 
United States. The HAC Task Force, an 
independent organization composed of 
groups who represent the interests of 
people with hearing loss, wireless 
service providers, and wireless handset 
manufacturers, was formed for the

on whether requiring 100% of all

hearing aid-compatible is an achievable 
objective. The HAC Task Force’s Final

recommendations for how the 
Commission can achieve this objective. 
We are committed to continuing to 
ensure that our wireless hearing aid 
compatibility provisions evolve to keep

ways handset models pair with hearing 
aids, and we will continue to monitor 
and update our hearing aid 
compatibility rules as circumstances 
warrant.

For Immediate Release
FCC REQUIRES ALL MOBILE PHONES TO BE HEARING AID 
COMPATIBLE
Rules Include New Bluetooth Requirements to Ensure Universal Connectivity
  -- 
WASHINGTON, October 17, 2024—The Federal Communications Commission today adopted 
new rules establishing that 100% of all mobile handsets—such as smartphones—must be 
compatible with hearing aids.  With this change, the 48 million Americans with hearing loss will 
be able to choose among the same mobile phone models that are available to all consumers.  
Under the new rules, after a transition period, Americans with hearing loss will no longer be 
limited in their choice of technologies, features, and prices available in the mobile handset 
marketplace.
The Commission also established a Bluetooth coupling requirement that will benefit consumers 
by ensuring more universal connectivity between mobile handsets and hearing aids, including 
over-the-counter hearing aids, by encouraging handset manufacturers to move away from 
proprietary Bluetooth coupling standards.
The Report and Order also requires that all new mobile handsets available in the U.S. must meet 
volume control benchmarks that ensure clear audio for the listener by allowing them to increase a 
mobile handset’s audio volume without introducing distortion.  Such requirements accommodate 
consumers with hearing loss who do not use hearing aids as well as those that rely on hearing aids 
or cochlear implants.
The new rules also revise labeling and website posting requirements to ensure consumers have 
access to the information that they need to make informed handset purchasing decisions.  Point-
of-sale labeling requirements will clarify if the handset is certified as hearing aid compatible, 
whether or not the handset meets telecoil or Bluetooth coupling requirements, and provide the 
handset’s conversational gain (i.e., how high the handset’s audio volume can be raised while still 
meeting volume control requirements).
Establishing a 100% hearing aid compatibility requirement for all mobile handsets was made 
possible by the collaborative efforts of members of the Hearing Aid Compatibility Task Force—
an independent organization of wireless service providers, handset manufacturers, research 
institutions and advocates for those with hearing loss.  Members of the Task Force worked 
together over a period of years to reach a consensus on how the Commission could achieve its 
objective of requiring 100% of all mobile handsets to be hearing aid compatible.
Action by the Commission October 17, 2024 by Report and Order (FCC 24-112).  Chairwoman 
Rosenworcel, Commissioners Carr, Starks, Simington, and Gomez approving.  Chairwoman 
Rosenworcel and Commissioner Starks issuing separate statements.

Federal Communications Commission FCC 24-112
STATEMENT OF
CHAIRWOMAN JESSICA ROSENWORCEL
Re:Achieving 100% Wireless Handset Model Hearing Aid Compatibility, WT Docket No. 23-388, 
Report & Order (October 17, 2024)
Hearing loss is a big deal.  In the United States, more than 48 million people have some form of 
hearing difficulty.  Among older adults it is especially prevalent, and it is also very common among 
veterans.  So the chances are you know someone impacted by hearing loss.    
The good news is that hearing aids and other technologies that can help those with hearing loss 
are more advanced, accessible, and affordable than ever before.  Two years ago, the Food and Drug 
Administration issued a landmark ruling, making it possible for the first time for hearing aids to be sold 
over-the-counter without a prescription.  Just last month, the FDA approved the use of new technology 
that will allow popular wireless headphones to be used as hearing aids.  These actions are powerful 
because they are expanding consumer choice and lowering consumer cost. 
So I believe now is the right time for the Federal Communications Commission to build on these 
efforts and finally deliver on a promise it made nearly a decade ago.  Back in 2016, the agency adopted a 
collaborative plan to improve access to mobile wireless handsets that are compatible with hearing aids.  
The goal was to make them widely available, so that people with hearing loss could use their phones 
without interference to their hearing aids or unwanted noise during conversations.  Today, we take the 
final step in that plan.  We ensure that all mobile wireless handsets available in the United States will be 
hearing aid compatible.  That means going forward, 100 percent of wireless phones will be capable of 
working seamlessly with hearing aids.  Even better, we are improving the way these devices will work 
with hearing aids in the future.  We clear the way for the use of new Bluetooth technologies that will help 
the growing number of new hearing aid options connect to mobile phones.  We also adopt a volume 
control requirement for handsets that will benefit all consumers with hearing loss, even those who do not 
use hearing aids.  
We are reaching this 100 percent milestone because a lot of stakeholders worked with us to build 
consensus.  In fact, many carriers and manufacturers have already contributed to this effort with a 
majority of handsets on the market today compatible with hearing aids.  But today we finish the job.   
To get to this point, we relied on the work of the Hearing Aid Compatibility Task Force, which 
brought together the expertise of equipment manufacturers, wireless carriers, research institutions and 
advocates for those with hearing loss to help make this happen.  I am grateful for the knowledge and 
persistence of all its members, including Linda Kozma-Spytek and Lise Hamlin who join us today.  I am 
also grateful to the staff who worked on this initiative, including Joel Taubenblatt, Barbara Esbin, John 
Lockwood, Kimia Nikseresht, Garnet Hanly, Susannah Larson, Eli Johnson, Jennifer Salhus, and Saurbh 
Chhabra from the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau; Robert Aldrich, Stephen Wang, Joshua 
Mendelsohn and Michael Scott from the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau; Ryan McDonald, 
Regina Brown, Neal McNeil, and Pamera Hairston from the Enforcement Bureau; Dana Shaffer, Jamison 
Prime, Jim Szeliga, Justin Rison, Reza Biazaran, and Jamie Coleman from the Office of Engineering and 
Technology; Donald Stockdale, Catherine Matraves, Kenneth Lynch, Weiren Wang, Molly Schwartz, 
Pramesh Jobanputra, Zaira Gonzalez, and Craig Stroup from the Office of Economics and Analytics; 
Douglas Klein, Anjali Singh, Bill Huber, and David Konczal from the Office of General Counsel; and 
Michael Gussow and Chana Wilkerson From the Office of Communications Business Opportunities.

STATEMENT OF
COMMISSIONER GEOFFREY STARKS
Re:Achieving 100% Wireless Handset Model Hearing Aid Compatibility, WT Docket No. 23-388, 
Report & Order (October 17, 2024)
As I said when I voted for last year’s hearing aid compatibility Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: 
“everyone in America deserves access to modern communications.”  With this Report and Order, we’re 
taking an important step toward ensuring that vision is a reality for the millions of Americans who depend 
on hearing aids. 
For years the Commission has been working to make sure every single smartphone sold in 
America can be used with a hearing aid – 100% compatibility.  Today that goal is finally within reach.  
By adopting a 100% hearing aid compatibility requirement to all future wireless handsets, we are 
delivering meaningful choice to the 48 million Americans with hearing loss.  This item is the result of 
years of collaboration among industry, consumer groups, standards organizations, and of course 
government.  I want to extend a particular thanks to the staff of the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau 
who worked tirelessly on this item. It has my full support.

Office of Engineering and Technology Announces Release
of Revised Supplement C to GET Bulletin 65
The Commission's Office of Engineering and Technology has released Edition 01-01 of
Supplement C to GET Bulletin 65 "Evaluating Compliance with FCC Guidelines for
Human Exposure to Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields." This revised edition,
which replaces Edition 97-01, provides additional guidance and information for
evaluating compliance of mobile and portable devices with FCC limits for
radiofrequency (RF) exposure.
Since 1997, Standards Coordinating Committee 34, Subcommittee 2, of the Institute of
Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Inc. (IEEE SCC-34/SC-2) has been developing
standard recommended procedures for evaluating portable devices using measurement or
computational methods. While this task has not yet been completed, sufficient consensus
now exists among industry experts to allow incorporation of the bulk of the committee's
work into Supplement C. Pending adoption of a formal industry standard, this revised
version of Supplement C provides standardized guidance for performing Specific
Absorption Rate (SAR) measurements on portable devices, as well as updated guidance
for other measurement-based and computational methods for evaluating RF exposure.
With the establishment of this standardized guidance, the Commission will now be able
to allow Telecommunications Certification Bodies (TCBs) to process certain applications
for equipment authorization containing RF exposure evaluations. Training of the TCBs in
RF exposure evaluation techniques will be conducted on August 27, 28 and 29, 2001, in
Columbia, MD, in cooperation with the TCB Council. Additional information regarding
the time and location of the training will be sent to TCBs in the near future. Following
training of TCBs, we anticipate allowing TCBs to start processing such applications by
October 1, 2001. This, along with continued processing of such apphcations by the
FCC's Laboratory Division, will allow alternative paths to approval for equipment
manufacturers, ensuring improvement in time-to-market for new devices.

Introduction - Purpose
Applies to § 15.202 Part 15 master transmitters that can automatically 
determine that their location is within the US and its territories and have the 
capability of deterring locations in other jurisdictions under differing RF 
governing authority and operate on frequencies and or power outside of their 
grant condition.
Enables manufacturers to market in the US and globally, a single hardware 
configuration or SKU.
This PIA does not apply to any device that uses Geolocation for other 
jurisdictions that complies with their FCC grant conditions for all locations 
worldwide.

because they are either new technology or new 
policy and the FCC reviews these PAG 
applications until such a time when the Labs and 
TCBs are both familiar and proficient with these 
PAG items.

specific guidance given in Workshop

TCB PROGRAM ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES 
1. INTRODUCTION 
The Telecommunication Certification Body (TCB) program was established in 1998 and updated in 20141 
as part of the equipment authorization program for equipment subject to the Commission’s certification 
procedures.  A TCB is an FCC-recognized ISO/IEC 170652 entity, which is authorized by the FCC to issue 
grants of equipment certification bearing a unique FCC ID, within its scope of recognition.3  TCBs have the 
authority to review and grant an application for certification for a product subject to the FCC certification rules.4  
The rules also established procedures for the recognition of foreign TCBs under the terms of a government-to-
government Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA).  The Commission will not recognize a TCB owned, 
controlled, or subject to influence of a prohibited entity, per Section 2.960(b) of the rules. 
2. KEY ROLES 
Accreditation Body (AB).  An AB is an independent, authorized organization that operates in accordance 
with the requirements of ISO/IEC 17011.5  ABs evaluate, assess, and accredit TCBs, which functions as a 
Conformity Assessment Body, in accordance with ISO/IEC 17065 and applicable FCC requirements. 
Accreditation is a third-party attestation of competence, capability, impartiality, and consistent operation 
of a TCB.  The AB shall notify TCBs that the confidentiality of ISO/IEC 17065 assessment records 
(including non-conformity reports) cannot be guaranteed, as such records may be requested by the FCC.. 
 
TCB Designating Authority (TDA).6  A TDA is a body responsible for recognizing ABs and for 
determining that an accredited TCB is competent and capable of reviewing and certifying devices within 
its designated FCC scopes.7  The TDA designates accredited TCBs to the FCC by uploading the required 
information to the FCC EAS8 database system. The TDA is responsible for notifying the FCC of any 
accreditation withdrawal, along with cause of such withdrawal, for any recognized TCB.  For accredited

DATA REFERENCING PROCEDURES

3.

4.

1. DATA REFERENCING BACKGROUND 
 
1.1 Introduction 
 
This publication provides guidance on the conditions under which applications for certification are 
permitted to demonstrate compliance by leveraging test data obtained from another device, a process known 
as Data Referencing.1 The referenced hardware, a fully populated device, is called the “parent” or “parent 
device”. The hardware device that is leveraging data from the parent device is called the “variant” or 
“variant device.” Data Referencing is limited to devices that use the same primary form factor build2 and 
share specific transmitter designs between them. Because a parent and its variants feature differences in 
hardware transmitters, they are all subject to separate certification applications under different FCC IDs. 
The parent certification shall demonstrate full compliance for all transmitters. All variants may only have 
one parent and demonstrate compliance with the same transmitter design used by the parent; this will be 
done by referencing the parent’s test report data and following the guidelines in this Data Referencing 
publication.  A variant may only contain transmitters that are included in the parent device. 
 
A typical example is that of a cellular handset, where the parent device could, for example, include a 
millimeter-wave transmitter under part 30 of the Commission’s rules, CMRS3 transmitters under parts 22, 
24, and 27, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth transmitters under part 15. The variant's millimeter wave transmitter is 
depopulated and removed but includes the same transmitter designs for parts 15, 22, 24, and 27 as used in 
the parent. 
 
1 The older terminology "data reuse" is deprecated in this context. 
2 “Same primary form factor build” indicates that variants are based on materials, form factors, printed circuit board 
(PCB) layouts, and components that are “very similar” the same as the parent device. The qualifier “very similar” is 
defined in detail in Section 2. 
3 CMRS: Commercial Mobile Radio Service. 

 
484596 Data Referencing Procedures DR01-46132 
Page 3 
In this context, a “grantee” refers to the entity to which the certification will be granted, typically the 
manufacturer; the Data Referencing process requires that a grantee (or an authorized representative of the 
grantee) develop a Data Referencing Plan document to be submitted to the TCB as part of the certification 
application. That document must clearly define the differences between the parent and all variants and 
provide all the relevant technical information and rule parts considered for certification (e.g., bands, 
emission designators, etc.). 
 
This publication provides guidance for developing the Data Referencing Plan required for submission to 
TCBs and for presenting referenced data in variant test report exhibits. 
 
Data Referencing, in the context of this publication, implies that some compliance test data obtained from 
the parent device is also sufficient to demonstrate compliance for the variant. The primary purpose of 
requiring “spot-checks” (details are provided in Section 3) is to establish that the maximum deviations from 
the parent data are within the acceptable range for the variants.  
 
Unlike previous practice,4 the TCB now manages the process entirely, including review of the Data 
Referencing Plan. 
 
1.2 Basis and Availability as an Optional Process 
 
Data Referencing is an optional process.  As part of its administration of the part 2 equipment authorization 
rules, OET recognizes that there are situations where a new equipment authorization application is required 
to be filed,5 but that the submission of certain test reports required under Section 2.10336 may be 
unnecessarily burdensome when an applicant can satisfactorily demonstrate compliance by leveraging test 
data obtained from another device.   
 
Data Referencing is strictly limited to what is allowed according to this publication. Grantees and TCBs 
are cautioned that changes in a variant that may impact RF field patterns can significantly increase non-
compliance risk and potentially lead to FCC post-grant certification dismissal.  
 
Applicants are always permitted to submit original test reports (i.e., without using referenced data) for 
variant devices instead of using the Data Referencing process. 
 
1.3 Data Referencing vs. Permissive Changes 
 
The Data Referencing process is unrelated to the Permissive Change process7 and only involves parents 
and variants, each with a separate FCC ID. More specifically, no Data Referencing process is applicable 
for device models/versions certified under the same FCC ID. Those cases are managed in the initial 
certification process and typically require complete testing of all the RF devices covered under the same 
FCC ID. 
 
 
 
 
 
4 Publications “484596 D01 Referencing Test Data” issued before v03. 
5 See 47 CFR § 2.932(a). 
6 See 47 CFR § 2.1033. 
7 Permissive changes apply to specific device under the same FCC ID, with limitations discussed in KDB Publication 
178919.

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
The Part 15 Geolocation General Persistent Inquiry Acceptance1 (PIA) applies to Part 15 master 
transmitters defined in § 15.2022 that use automated geolocation methods to determine whether operation 
occurs within the United States or its territories. When a device determines it is operating outside the U.S. 
regulatory area, it is no longer required to comply with its FCC grant conditions and may instead operate 
under the regulations of the governing authority in that region. This enables manufacturers to globally 
market a single hardware configuration or SKU3 across jurisdictions with differing RF requirements. 
 
This PIA outlines the information manufacturers must include in Part 15 Geolocation General PIA 
submission. Once accepted, it may be used in subsequent equipment certification applications.  
Devices that use geolocation solely to manage operation in other regulatory regions—and whose 
transmissions always comply with their FCC grant conditions—are not subject to the Part 15 Geolocation 
General PIA. In these cases, geolocation features serve only to meet non‑U.S. regulatory requirements, as 
all emissions remain within the limits authorized for U.S. operation. 
 
This PIA addresses Part 15 Geolocation General submissions only. It does not cover other geolocation-
based PIAs, for example, the 6 GHz AFC4  which has separate PIA requirements and procedures. 
 
 
 
1 A PIA is a process that, under certain conditions, allows applicants to refer, repeatedly over time, to a previously 
approved KDB inquiry. Reference KDB Publication 951290 Equipment Compliance Review. 
2 47 CFR § 15.202 Certified operating frequency range. A master is a device that can initiate a transmission and 
transmit without receiving an enabling signal. 
3 SKU or stock keeping unit is the unit of identification in which the products are managed. It is a distinct type of item 
for sale, purchase, or tracking in inventory. In this description it is referring to the specific product build encompassing 
its design, parts, specifications and features as sold. 
4 Reference: 987594 D01 U-NII 6GHz General Requirements v03r01 

594280 Part 15 Geolocation General PIA-DR01-46099 
Page 3 
2. PIA PROCEDURE 
 
Manufacturers or grantees using automated geolocation techniques to determine device location for 
compliance with U.S. rules may submit a Persistent Inquiry Acceptance (PIA) request to the FCC for 
review and acceptance through the Knowledge Database (KDB) inquiry system. To do this, they must 
attach a PDF titled “Part 15 General Description PIA” that describes their geolocation method (document 
requirements are provided in Section III below). When submitting the inquiry, applicants must select 
Category 1: Equipment Compliance Review and Category 2: Part 15 Geolocation General PIA.  
 
The FCC will review this “Part 15 Geolocation General PIA” document and, if approved, issue an 
acceptance letter under the inquiry tracking number associated” with the PIA. Both the “Part 15 General 
Description” document and the FCC acceptance letter will be returned to the party that submitted the PIA, 
these documents must be provided to the Telecommunications Certification Body (TCB) when applying 
for equipment certification for products using this automated geolocation techniques. 
 
Both the – General Description document and acceptance letter are public exhibits. If confidentiality is 
required for the general description, the manufacture shall provide an additional document—a “scrubbed” 
version with confidential information removed—as an “Overview of “Part 15 Geolocation General PIA”. 
In that case the “Part 15 General Description” may be held confidential with justification, subject to the 
Commission’s confidentiality rules5. 
 
3. GUIDANCE FOR OVERVIEW OF “PART 15 GEOLOCATION GENERAL PIA” 
DOCUMENT. 
 
The “Part 15 Geolocation General PIA” supporting documentation shall consist of the following five 
sections: 
 
3.1 Attestation Statement  
Manufacturers shall provide a statement of compliance consistent with the following example: 
 
I, ‘name / company’, attest that all devices seeking certification under 47 CFR Part 2, Subpart J using this 
Geolocation-General PIA employ the geolocation control system, internal regulatory tables, and security 
protections as described in this document. 
 
3.2 General Overview of the Geolocation Method  
Manufacturers shall provide a clear and concise overview explaining how the RF device determines its 
operating location and automatically enforces power and operational constraints based on the applicable 
regulatory zone. 
 
The description must clearly identify the type of device being controlled, including how it fits into one of 
the following categories: 
 
• 
Fixed devices: Permanently installed at a known, stationary location. 
• 
Transportable but ac‑powered devices: Equipment that may be moved between locations but 
operates only when connected to fixed AC mains power. 
 
5 Inquiry shall provide the Justification in accordance with 47 CFR §§ 0.457(d) and 0.45 for requesting the information 
be held confidential and the methods used to prevent unauthorized disclosure as public information.

ACCREDITED TESTING LABORATORY PROGRAM 
ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES 
 
1. INTRODUCTION 
The FCC equipment authorization program as detailed in Part 2 Subpart J1 has two approval procedures: 
certification and Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity (SDoC).2  The approval procedure required to be 
used is specified in the applicable FCC rule part(s) that apply to the radio frequency functions of a device 
or an end-product.  In general, except when otherwise stated in a rule, intentional radiators (transmitters) 
are required to be approved using the Certification procedure, and unintentional radiators (e.g. digital 
circuitry) are approved using the SDoC procedure. 
 
Certification constitutes the most rigorous equipment authorization procedure,3 and requires that 
compliance testing be performed at an FCC-recognized accredited testing laboratory.4  The accreditation 
is performed by an FCC-recognized accreditation body, or an accreditation body recognized under the 
terms of a government-to-government Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA).  FCC recognized testing 
laboratories can be found by searching on the Commission’s website.5  The website also contains a 
searchable database containing applications for Certification along with associated test reports and other 
supporting information.  When using the SDoC procedure, testing is not required to be performed by an 
FCC-recognized accredited testing laboratory. 
 
2. KEY ROLES6 
Accreditation Body.  An Accreditation Body (AB) is an independent, authorized organization that 
operates based on ISO/IEC 17011 competence and impartiality standards.  ABs evaluate, assess, and 
accredit testing laboratories (Conformity Assessment Bodies) in accordance with ISO/IEC 17025 and 
FCC requirements.  Accreditation is a third-party attestation of competence, capability, impartiality, and 
consistent operation of a conformity assessment body.7 
 
 
1 See 47 CFR. Part 2 Subpart J. 
2 On July 13, 2017, the FCC adopted Report and Order FCC 17-93 that merged the Declaration of Conformity (DoC) 
and verification procedures into the new Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity (SDoC) procedure.   
3 See 47 CFR. § 2.907. 
4 See 47 CFR § 2.950.  All testing performed on applications for certification are required to be based on testing 
performed by an FCC-recognized accredited testing laboratory. 
5 The Commission’s Equipment Authorization System (EAS) database can be accessed at 
https://apps.fcc.gov/oetcf/eas/reports/GenericSearch.cfm.   
6 We note that a device evaluated by a testing laboratory for FCC Certification or SDoC also involves the 
Responsible Party, as defined in § 2.909, even though the Responsible Party is not directly involved in the 
laboratory accreditation activities discussed herein. 
7 See ISO/IEC 17000:2004, 2.6 and 5.6; the authority of an accreditation body is typically derived from a 
government body. 

 
974614 D01 Accredited Test Lab Roles and Resp DR01-46076 
Page 3 
Designating Authority.  A Designating Authority (DA) is a body responsible for determining that a 
testing laboratory is competent and capable of performing testing within the scope of its designation.8  
The DA designates accredited testing laboratories to the FCC by uploading the required information to 
the FCC database.  The DA is also responsible for notifying the FCC of any accreditation withdrawal, 
along with the reason for withdrawal, for any FCC-recognized laboratory.  
 
Testing laboratory.  For a device under test, the testing laboratory is responsible for determining the 
applicable rule parts, operational conditions, compliance requirements, perform the applicable testing, and 
issue the test report(s) demonstrating the device compliance. 
 
3. ACCREDITED TESTING LABORATORY RECOGNITION PROCEDURE 
The following procedure is used for a testing laboratory to be recognized by the FCC as an accredited 
testing laboratory, and to be deemed competent to test products subject to the certification approval 
procedure.9 
 
3.1 Step 1 – Laboratory Accreditation 
1) The testing laboratory must seek accreditation from one of the Test Firm Accrediting Bodies 
listed on the FCC accredited test firm webpage.  
2) Obtain ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation with a scope covering the applicable FCC requirements and 
test methods identified in Table A1 of this document.10  
3) The accreditation body (AB) will use the “Accredited Testing Laboratory FCC Technical 
Assessment Checklist” to assist in the assessment of the testing laboratory.11   
3.2 Step 2 – Designation 
1) Once the accreditation process in 3.1 is complete, a request (designation) for recognition may be 
submitted to the FCC by uploading supporting information to the FCC database.  The party 
submitting the request is known as the designating authority (DA).   
2) For accredited testing laboratories in the U.S. or in non-MRA countries, the DA is the FCC-
recognized AB.   
3) For accrediting bodies in MRA countries, the DA is defined in the MRA.  In MRA countries, the 
DA reviews the accreditation information and decides as to whether the testing laboratory meets 
the requirements for designation.  Once the DA determines that the requirements have been met, 
it designates the accredited testing laboratory to the FCC by providing the supporting information 
listed in 3.4 for review and recognition by the FCC.  
3.3 Step 3 – FCC Recognition 
1) The FCC will review the information submitted regarding the testing laboratory.   
2) The FCC will make a determination on whether to recognize the testing laboratory. 
 
8 See ISO/IEC 17000:2004, 7.3. 
9 The use of an FCC-recognized accredited testing laboratory is not required for products subject to the verification 
or Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity (SDoC) approval procedures.  However, the testing laboratory is required to 
maintain a record of their measurement facilities as required in § 2.948. 
10 The Commission will accept ISO/IEC 17025:2017, incorporated by reference under 2.910. 
11  See KDB Publication 853844.

may be evaluated and documented by the assessor(s).  The accreditation body shall attest that all 
responses in this checklist are complete and accurate.  The completed checklist for each laboratory shall 
be submitted (uploaded) to the FCC, and will be made publicly available.

CFR § 15.31.  A list of measurement procedures is also found on the FCC equipment authorization 
measurements page at: https://www.fcc.gov/oet/ea/eameasurements.html or 
https://www.fcc.gov/general/equipment-authorization-measurement-procedures.  Finally, the FCC OET 
Knowledge Database (https://www.fcc.gov/kdb) provides additional guidance on testing devices subject 
to the FCC's rules.

the testing laboratory to be recognized by the FCC, each laboratory must be assessed and found 
competent to perform testing with all applicable parts of each standard for which FCC scope recognition

SIGNAL BOOSTERS BASIC CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS 
I. INTRODUCTION
In Report and Order FCC 13-21 (WT Docket No. 10-4, referred to as “the Order”), the Commission 
outlined equipment authorization and operational requirements for signal boosters operating under Parts 
20, 22, 24, 27, and 90 of the FCC rules.[R3]-[R7]1  The Order created two classes of signal boosters, 
Consumer and Industrial, with specific regulatory requirements for each class.  Part 90 PLMR signal 
boosters, a special type of Industrial Boosters, have additional unique requirements.  In 2014 and 2015, 
various consumer booster rules were also updated by an Order on Reconsideration (FCC 14-138 [R12]).  
The Second Report and Order FCC 18-35 ([R22], [R23]) modified personal-use conditions for Provider-
Specific Consumer Signal Boosters.   
This document provides a summary of the rules related to equipment authorization, as well as additional 
policies and guidance for certification applications.  Due to the significant changes from the preceding 
rules and with the intended new framework, manufacturers, test labs, and TCBs are encouraged to submit 
KDB inquiries to request clarification and guidance before starting compliance testing or preparing an 
equipment authorization application where the available policies and test procedures do not readily 
support review and approval of a specific booster device. 
For equipment operation, boosters must also comply with applicable service rules that apply to the bands 
of operation, in addition to those specified in the Order.  For equipment authorization, booster test reports 
must address all applicable requirements in Part 2 and the respective rule parts for the band of operations, 
in addition to the requirements listed in sections II to V of this document. 
Compliance testing procedures are provided in KDB Publication 935210 Attachment D03 for Wideband 
Consumer Signal Boosters, in KDB Publication 935210 Attachment D04 for Provider-Specific Consumer 
Signal Boosters, and in KDB Publication 935210 Attachment D05 for Industrial Signal Boosters (CMRS 
and PLMRS2) and non-consumer repeater and amplifier devices.

herein; Part 90 Subpart B) and the Industrial/Business Radio Pool (Part 90 Subpart C).

APPLICATION PROGRAMMING INTERFACE (API) FOR OET EQUIPMENT 
AUTHORIZATION SYSTEM 
1. OVERVIEW  
This publication describes the functions supported by the Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) for 
the OET Equipment Authorization System (EAS). The API currently has four method calls: 
getFCCIDList, getWhitespaceAuthorizations, getCBSDAuthorizations, and getAFCAuthorizations. The 
following sections describe the details of the functions supported and the input and output fields. The 
getFCCIDList call takes a full or partial FCC ID as a parameter and returns any matching approved 
equipment authorizations on file with the OET Laboratory. A call to getWhitespaceAuthorizations, 
getCBSDAuthorizations, or getAFCAuthorizations takes a starting and ending date range as parameters. 
It returns the FCC IDs for the approved equipment class(s) for equipment either for Whitespace, CBSD, 
or AFC, respectively, within that date range provided in the call. 
2. DESCRIPTIONS OF THE SERVICES  
getFCCIDList: API allows users to enter a grantee code or the initial portion of an FCC ID and obtain a 
list of all granted FCC IDs that are an exact or partial match.  The minimum search criterion that must be 
entered is a three or five-character grantee code.  The return results include a list of FCC IDs that match 
the search parameters entered, the grant date and application purpose for each FCC ID, and the grantee 
name and address.  
getWhitespaceAuthorizations: API allows users to obtain a list of all white space equipment 
authorizations subject to Certification that have been approved over the specified date range.  The date is 
entered in the format MM-DD-YYYY.  A start and end date are both required.  The results returned 
identify the FCC ID, Equipment Class, Status, Status Date, and Application Purpose.  This includes 
equipment classes for White Space devices (Fixed, Equipment Class WGF; Personal/Portable (P/P) 
Mode II, Equipment Class WG2; Mobile, Equipment class WMO; Narrowband White Space, Equipment 
Class WIT) authorized under CFR 47 Part 15 Subpart H and Knowledge Data Base (KDB1) 416721 
getCBSDAuthorizations: API allows users to obtain a list of all Citizens Broadband Radio Service 
Device equipment authorizations subject to Certification that have been approved over the specified date 
range. The date is entered in the format MM-DD-YYYY.  A start and end date are both required.  The 
return results include the Application Purpose, Equipment Class, FCC ID, Grantee Name, Status, Status 
Date, Grant Notes, Description, Emission Designator, Frequency Max, Frequency Min, and Power 
Output.  The results returned include all equipment authorizations under the equipment classes CBD-
Citizens Band Category A and B Devices, and CBE-Citizens Band End User devices authorized under 
CFR 47 Part 96 H and Knowledge Data Base (KDB) 940660 
getAFCAuthorizations: API allows users to obtain a list of all standard access points and fixed client 
devices that have been certified over the specified date range.  The date is entered in the format 
MM-DD-YYYY.  A start and end date are both required.  The return results include the Application 
Purpose, Equipment Class, FCC ID, Grantee Name, Status, Status Date, Grant Notes, Description, 
Frequency Max, Frequency Min, and Power Output.  The return results include all equipment 
authorizations under the equipment classes 6SD for a Standard Power Access Point and 6FC for Fixed 
Client devices authorized under CFR 47 Part 15 Subpart E and Knowledge Data Base (KDB) 987594.

SAR TESTING FOR IRREGULAR SHAPED DEVICES 
1. INTRODUCTION
The shape of a device may prevent a test lab from performing SAR testing on the transmit antennas at a 
distance that conservatively represents actual use conditions.  Testing at distances further than those 
experienced by the end user fails to comply with the RF exposure rules and published guidance.   
Examples of devices with unusual and irregular shapes include, but are not limited to, game controllers, 
RFID scanners, and wearables such as watches, eyeglasses, and similar items.  
The purpose of this document is to provide both general and device-specific guidance to test labs 
performing SAR testing when conventional testing methods may be impractical for certain devices.  
2. GENERAL GUIDANCE
SAR measurement procedures are outlined in KDB Publication 865664 D01, which provides general 
guidelines for performing SAR measurements. 
For devices with an irregular shape, it may be impossible to use the standard SAR phantoms as required.  
For example, devices designed to be held in the hand are generally tested on a flat phantom; however, 
there are many devices that contain large grips, thumb controls (e.g., joysticks), and other protrusions that 
may make testing impossible while attempting to use the appropriate separation distance.  To ensure a 
device is tested adequately, there are a few options available; the flow chart in Figure 1 illustrates how to 
test an irregularly shaped device for SAR (Figure 1).1 
When it is not possible to demonstrate compliance with the RF exposure limits due to device shape, the 
corners, curvatures, and other features of phantoms may be used for demonstrating compliance.  For 
example, a wearable device with a fixed strap that prevents direct placement against the flat phantom may 
be placed on the neck of the specific anthropomorphic mannequin (SAM) phantom.  This approach 
minimizes the separation distance between the phantom and the wearable device (W).   
1 KDB Publication 388624 D02 requires a PAG when nonstandard phantoms are used except when an approved PIA 
is available.

1. GENERAL 
Section 20.21 contains the rules for signal boosters (including DAS) generally, including those intended 
for Part 96 Citizens Broadband Radio Service operations. Testing shall generally follow KDB 
Publications 935210 D05, 935210 D02, and 940660 D01.1 
 
Applicable Part 96 equipment types: 
 
1) Citizens Broadband Radio Service Device (CBSD) requirements apply independent of device EIRP 
(EIRP density), including registering with and following SAS directions. 
2) Booster and DAS devices cannot be certified to Part 96 as an End User Device since these devices 
may not be used as intermediate service links (see definitions in Section 96.3), further to the Part 96 
definitions of an end-user device (EUD), and other device and station types definitions. Therefore, 
boosters (including DAS) under Part 96 shall be classified as a CBSD and use equipment class CBD. 
 
Terminology used to describe DAS booster equipment and its system components varies across 
manufacturers. The following abbreviations and terms are used for FCC equipment authorization 
purposes in accordance with this document. 
 
1) BBU – Baseband Unit: processes baseband signals and may be decomposed into CU+DU. 
2) DU – Distributed Unit: handles PHY, MAC & RLC layer tasks.  
3) CU – Centralized Unit: handles higher layer protocol functions.  
4) RU – Radio Unit (Radio Source): handles RF and lower physical layer signal processing.  
5) DP – Domain Proxy: intermediary entity that communicates with the SAS on behalf of CBSDs. 
6) SAS – Spectrum Access System 
7) TP – Transmission Point: Active or Passive elements used for over the air transmission/reception. 
a) Passive DAS: Network of spatially separated TPs comprised of only passive elements (feeders, 
splitters, diplexers, etc.) between the Radio Source and each of the TPs. 
b) Active DAS: Network of spatially separated TPs comprised of Active elements between Radio 
Source and each of the TPs. 
8) CPI – Certified Professional Installer 
9) CPRI – Common Public Radio Interface 
10) eCPRI – Enhanced Common Public Radio Interface 
11) RRH – Remote Radio Head
